Keep Grégoire’s constitutional Church, Catholic revival and state-sponsored alternatives distinct; clerical repression did not demonstrate disappearance of popular religion.

stage6_parent_bindings.meaning: Officially favoured Theophilanthropy offered urban deism with elite sponsorship and prominent former churches, while Grégoire maintained constitutional Catholic organization. Attempts to privilege décadi failed to displace broad Sunday observance; the new cult remained a minority movement.
stage6_parent_bindings.stance: Theophilanthropy receives prominent churches and elite sponsorship after Fructidor but never secures broad popular support or displaces Sunday worship.

stage6_parent_bindings.meaning: Reactivation of laws against nonjuror clergy, the oath of hatred for royalty, and deportations to Ré, Oléron, and Guiana. Refusal was concentrated in annexed Belgium, where fear of resistance constrained enforcement; people liable, island internees and those actually shipped to Guiana were different populations.
stage6_parent_bindings.stance: The repression is presented as a severe blow to the religious revival, but mass enforcement was constrained in annexed Belgium and actual transport to Guiana was limited.

stage6_parent_bindings.meaning: Jacobin press, clubs and parliamentary activity revived in distinct Directorial cycles: post-Vendémiaire indulgence aided the Pantheon Club before closure; post-Fructidor constitutional circles rallied mixed anti-royalist republicans before democratic demands prompted restriction. In1799 press freedom, the Manège, appointments and emergency conscription, forced-loan and hostage measures renewed influence without a parliamentary majority. Official encouragement again gave way to hostile campaigning, eviction and Fouché’s closure of the Manège; rejection of Country in Danger contained emergency politics and served Sieyes’s constitutional-executive project. Jacobin efforts to impeach the former Directors and General Schérer rested on accusations of corruption; the indictments were ultimately rejected, not established as judicial findings.
stage6_parent_bindings.stance: Pantheon, constitutional circles and Manège were distinct formations. Wartime emergency and anti-royalism created opportunities, but neither official encouragement nor electoral gains meant stable Jacobin control.

rows.lead_retention_check: The new cult’s elite sponsorship, Grégoire’s continuing Catholic organization and failed displacement of Sunday are explicit. Repression does not imply eradication of Catholic recovery.

stage6_parent_bindings.meaning: The neo-Jacobin electoral revival, systematic government interference, divided electoral assemblies, and the Law of 22 Floréal's purge of elected deputies. The outgoing legislature retained scrutiny of incoming elections, purged127deputies, quashed eight departmental results, seated preferred minorities and runners-up, and excluded86identifiable Jacobin winners.
stage6_parent_bindings.stance: Floréal was less spectacular and less decisive than Fructidor. It again denied electoral choice and preserved executive control, but some admitted as reliable later defected. Some historians think a viable opposition might have emerged in an unpurged legislature; that counterfactual is distinct from the actual later defections and from proving every excluded deputy moderate.

stage6_parent_bindings.stance: Low participation and weak protest facilitated manipulation, but were not positive consent to coups. Restored local autonomy and satisfaction with peace and victory also muted national resistance.

source_first_finding_and_prior_dispositi.source_first_requirement: French claims of superiority and natural frontiers underwrote Rhine annexation, sister republics and interference in Rome/Switzerland. Egypt, Malta, papal imprisonment and Russian/Austrian/Neapolitan interests converged in renewed war; Championnet’s expansion exceeded policy.
source_first_finding_and_prior_dispositi.independent_reconciliation: Expansion and coalition parents preserve varied territorial forms and motivations. Keep direct annexation separate from client republics, Malta/Egypt/Rome/Switzerland distinct, and Championnet’s initiative separate from a uniformly ordered central plan. Map interiors remain excluded.

stage6_parent_bindings.meaning: Continental victory and post-Floréal confidence encouraged the Great Nation’s claim to superior liberty, natural frontiers and entitlement to follow its own rules. Belgium’s occupation and annexation contrasted with dependent Italian republics; nominally republican institutions could conceal appointed rulers and military supremacy. Extraction, religious coercion and disregard of foreign traditions turned deference into resistance and helped renew coalition war. Foreign collaborators and reforms remained real, but support diminished; the1799 military reversal destroyed the Italian client system, not every sister republic everywhere.
stage6_parent_bindings.stance: The source criticizes nationally exclusive liberty and arrogance while recognizing institutional changes and native collaborators. Territorial form and degrees of control differed; loss of legitimacy was not proof that every reform had no value.

stage6_parent_bindings.meaning: French-sponsored republics varied in constitutional authorship and domestic autonomy. Dutch elected life and locally drafted Ligurian institutions differed from imposed Swiss unity, Bonaparte’s dictated Cisalpine constitution and initial nominees, and the Roman commandant’s explicit supremacy. Local reformers and French military or anti-clerical initiatives interacted; occupation, strategic access, fiscal obligations and repeated coups limited sovereignty. The Directory did not welcome every new satellite: Championnet’s independent Neapolitan creation depended on French troops and collapsed when they withdrew.
stage6_parent_bindings.stance: Do not flatten Dutch or Ligurian local initiative into the same model as imposed Swiss unity or Roman military supremacy. The Directory did not uniformly welcome every new satellite, but their spread deepened international alarm.

stage6_parent_bindings.meaning: After Fructidor ended Austrian hopes of exploiting French division, Campo Formio largely confirmed the earlier Leoben preliminaries: Belgium and Italian republics were recognized, Venice partitioned and France’s Rhine claims acknowledged by Austria. Austria could not bind the Holy Roman Empire, so compensatory German redistribution was deferred to Rastadt. The continental settlement left Britain at war and renewed coalition conflict already germinating.
stage6_parent_bindings.stance: Bonaparte largely dictated a settlement that confirmed French continental dominance but left Great Britain at war and future coalition conflict already germinating.

stage6_parent_bindings.meaning: The convergence of Ottoman, Russian, Neapolitan, Austrian, and other resistance to French expansion in 1798-1799 and the renewal of continental war. PaulI resented exclusion from Rastadt and French actions concerning Malta and Poland. Ottoman reaction to Egypt enabled Russian passage; Neapolitan action in Rome ended in retreat and royal flight. Austrian alarm and the failed ultimatum brought renewed war before the Rastadt murders marked the peace collapse.
stage6_parent_bindings.stance: A multi-causal coalition: French expansion, Egyptian aggression, Nelson’s victory, Russian grievances and Austrian alarm converged. Ottoman entry was politically consequential despite limited immediate military weight; the Rastadt murders marked the collapse of peace rather than single-handedly causing war.

stage6_parent_bindings.meaning: The Directory's strategic and political reasons for approving Bonaparte's Egyptian expedition, its initial conquests, and Nelson's destruction of the French fleet. Port and naval limitations frustrated the Channel invasion option. Bonaparte conceived Egypt as an indirect attack on British Indian wealth; Talleyrand supported the idea and they jointly proposed the expedition; the Directors expected either success abroad or failure that discredited an awkward general. Malta and Alexandria preceded the Pyramids victory and occupation of Cairo.
stage6_parent_bindings.stance: The project appeared cheaper and potentially decisive against Britain while removing a troubling general, but naval defeat nullified the lightning campaign, isolated the army, and catalyzed a new coalition.

rows.lead_retention_check: Great Nation and sister-republic meanings preserve variation, native collaborators, coercion and the Directory’s opposition to some satellites. The 1799 collapse is limited to the Italian client system, with multiple coalition motives.

source_first_finding_and_prior_dispositi.source_first_requirement: The law revived universal service obligation with volunteers first and annual classes of young men as needed. Renewed war and anticlericalism recalled earlier unpopular demands, eroding the prospect of stability and eventually military loyalty.
source_first_finding_and_prior_dispositi.independent_reconciliation: The Jourdan parent retains annual classes, continuing state obligation and resistance; final main content must preserve volunteers-first selection and broader political consequences. Do not misstate conscription as repealed after Brumaire or treat the prospective collapse argument on 340 as an already completed coup.

stage6_parent_bindings.meaning: The Jourdan Law of1798 established annual classes of citizens aged twenty to twenty-five available for defense when volunteers were insufficient. Full activation in1799 called eligible men in those classes and prohibited purchased substitutes, meeting military need while provoking evasion, desertion, royalist recruitment and banditry. Pressure continued beyondBrumaire and eased with peace.
stage6_parent_bindings.stance: Recruitment answered military need while reviving memories of coercive mobilization. It was not one of the civil measures repealed after Brumaire: keep it separate from the forced loan and hostage law.

stage6_parent_bindings.meaning: The Directory sought a propertied republican centre between royalism and Jacobinism but alternated cultivation and repression, manipulated elections and relied increasingly on soldiers. Fiscal reconstruction alienated its intended supporters. It failed to organize its own moderate party or recognize legitimate opposition, while royalist restorationism and Jacobin associations with the YearII also obstructed compromise. Renewed war, religious coercion and conscription returned unresolved conflicts; popular abstention and silence concealed loss of confidence rather than stable consent. Constitutional failure arose from political practice and intolerance as well as institutional tensions. Belief that all honest citizens shared one general will made organized parties appear illegitimate factions, an ideological obstacle to accepting representative competition.
stage6_parent_bindings.stance: The constitution was not simply doomed by design: political actors refused to let it operate freely. Threats from both extremes were real, but repeated preemption destroyed trust and abstention cannot be read as positive consent.

stage6_parent_bindings.meaning: The growing use of soldiers and successful generals as the regime's indispensable instruments of domestic order, electoral control, and survival. Vendémiaire ended Parisian coercive primacy; dissolution of the suspect Police Legion increased military dependence. In1797the generals’ conquest interests and partisan addresses helped the divided executive override the legislature; the chapter’s closing forecast anticipates, rather than narrates as complete, the army abandoning the regime.
stage6_parent_bindings.stance: The chapter emphasizes that military dependence was foundational, deepened through repression and coups, and ultimately undermined civilian constitutional authority.

proposed_record.label: Émigré counter-revolution: organization, foreign dependence and failed army
proposed_record.meaning: The princes and émigrés attempted propaganda, diplomacy and armed restoration, linking Artois and Calonne’s Turin court to Catholic resistance at Jalès and the failed Lyons conspiracy before relocating to Koblenz. Successive emigrant waves and noble and clerical grievances shaped the movement. Military formations existed before Varennes; the flight accelerated officer emigration and militarization. Sincere loyalty and personal sacrifice coexisted with rank rivalry, weak finance and supply, unrealistic promises of foreign help and dependence on foreign strategy. Retreat after Valmy dispersed the principal émigré army; Condé’s surviving corps was an exception.
proposed_record.stance: Do not treat émigrés as a homogeneous force or the agents of western peasant revolt. Their political claims exceeded resources and dependable foreign commitment; Condé’s survival was an exception to wider military collapse.

evidence.evidence_summary: Catholic organizers at Jalès coordinated with agents of the Count d'Artois, who envisioned armed intervention from Turin.
Catholic leaders from Nîmes took over a Guard federation, denounced Protestant control, preserved an organizing committee, and contacted Artois’s agents.
Agents of Artois connected with Jalès organizers while he imagined armed rescue and revolutionary reversal.
Before 1790 counter-revolution had little existence beyond the émigré court; by late 1790 its agents planned a Rhône valley rising.
Artois and Calonne sought to rescue the monarchy and restore aristocratic power, using agents among Catholic leaders and planning a Rhône uprising.
He increasingly followed Calonne and sought a Rhône-wide rising despite limited royal cooperation.
The Lyons plot was exposed, the second Jalès camp failed, and the émigré headquarters shifted from Turin to Koblenz.
A second camp failed to rally decisive forces and was bloodily dispersed by a largely Protestant force.
Discovery of the Lyons papers and failure at Jalès exposed poor security and coordination.
Diplomatic embarrassment forced the émigré court from Turin; it re-established itself at Koblenz.
Louis XVI asked him to abandon the Lyons plan, and diplomatic pressure later displaced his court from Turin.
Near constitutional completion the king again urged Artois to return and stop plotting.
The émigré princes helped publicize Pillnitz and urged Louis XVI to reject the constitution, intensifying invasion fears.
Traces the first emigration after July 1789, frontier committees, and Artois's Turin organization.
Abolition of nobility, military mutinies and abolition of the parlements drew nobles, officers and magistrates into continued emigration; clerical departures are described on300.
Varennes accelerated officer departures and transformed émigré rescue ambitions.
The Black Legion and Ardennes drilling preceded Varennes; incoming officers then intensified militarization at Koblenz, where the army still expected to serve as an auxiliary to foreign forces.
Exile courts reproduced precedence disputes and suspicion of latecomers; the portrait is qualified by recognition of sacrifice.
Loyalty and risk qualified the portrait of selfish exile; subsidies, supply failure, disbandment, and refusal of amnesty reveal practical weakness.
The retreat after Valmy shattered princely formations; Condé alone retained a corps in imperial service and émigrés dispersed.
Concludes that feuding émigrés had no independent chance of arresting, moderating, or reversing events in France.
Post-1792 émigration brought constitutional monarchists into sharper conflict with restorationist pures.

proposed_record.meaning: La Rouërie organized the Breton Association through coastal contacts and links to émigré princes, driven by opposition to the loss of Brittany’s distinct provincial character and encouraged by widespread support for refractory clergy.
